claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a ferrite–pearlite microstructure.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide layer.
The native oxide on Q235 steel is an effective corrosion barrier at room temperature.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, the oxide on Q235 steel undergoes phase transformation and spallation.
High-temperature oxide transformation and spallation compromise the integrity of the Q235 oxide layer.
Loss of oxide integrity permits increased salt penetration and accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
A suitable high-alloy stainless-steel reference forms a robust and stable Cr-rich oxide.
At room temperature, the native oxide on Q235 remains continuous and self-healing.
At high temperature, reactive salt causes the Q235 oxide to change through phase transformation, growth, or spallation.
Q235 steel will exhibit minimal mass loss and stable oxide characteristics during room-temperature salt exposure.
Q235 steel will exhibit increased mass loss and observable oxide transformation or spallation during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The high-alloy stainless-steel reference will retain a stable Cr-rich oxide under the high-temperature salt exposure.
Untreated Q235 steel has adequate passivation during room-temperature salt exposure.
Annealing or coating may alter the oxide properties enough that the proposed mechanism no longer applies.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to salts having reactivity different from the specified NaCl-based environment.
High-temperature salt exposure can cause phase instability in a Cr–Mn–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy.
Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 loses significantly more mass than 316H stainless steel after exposure to molten FLiBe at 700 °C for 1000 hours.
The excess mass loss of the Cr–Mn–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy was attributed to Mn dissolution into molten FLiBe rather than oxide transformation or spallation.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism attributes degradation to oxide transformation, spallation, and salt penetration, whereas the cited high-temperature study attributes mass loss in a different alloy and salt system to Mn dissolution and reports bulk Cr-rich precipitation rather than oxide-film failure.
